_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Present (polite)
entries.usage: What happens now or regularly — the everyday 요-form.
entries.example: 저는 학교에 가요. — I go to school.

entries.label: Past
entries.usage: What already happened: 았/었 slides in before the ending.
entries.example: 어제 학교에 갔어요. — I went to school yesterday.

entries.label: Future
entries.usage: Plans and predictions with (으)ㄹ 거예요.
entries.example: 내일 학교에 갈 거예요. — I will go to school tomorrow.

entries.label: Formal ㅂ니다
entries.usage: The news-and-business register: 갑니다, 먹습니다.
entries.example: 저는 매일 회사에 갑니다. — I go to the office every day.

entries.point: Ongoing and resulting: 고 있어요 / 아·어 있어요 (자고 있어요)
entries.label: Progressive
entries.usage: In the middle of doing: 고 있어요.
entries.example: 지금 밥을 먹고 있어요. — I'm eating right now.

entries.label: Can / can't
entries.usage: Ability and impossibility with (으)ㄹ 수 있어요/없어요.
entries.example: 저는 한국어를 할 수 있어요. — I can speak Korean.

entries.point: Must and may: 아/어야 해요, 아/어도 돼요 (가야 해요)
entries.label: Must / may
entries.usage: Obligation (야 해요) and permission (도 돼요).
entries.example: 지금 집에 가야 해요. — I have to go home now.

entries.point: Irregular verbs: ㅂ, ㄷ, 르 (추워요, 들어요, 몰라요)
entries.label: Irregular stems
entries.usage: The ㅂ/ㄷ/르 families transform before vowel endings: 춥다 → 추워요.
entries.example: 오늘 날씨가 정말 추워요. — The weather is really cold today.

entries.point: Honorific machinery: 께서, 드리다, 뵙다 (선생님께서 말씀하셨어요)
entries.label: Honorific forms
entries.usage: Raising the subject with 께서 + 시, humbling yourself with 드리다/뵙다.
entries.example: 선생님께서 오셨어요. — The teacher has arrived.

entries.label: Copula 이다
entries.usage: Attach 이다 / 야·이야 / 예요·이에요 to a noun to say 'X is Y'.
entries.example: 이것은 책이에요.

entries.point: Present Tense Conjugation of 이다 / 아니다
entries.label: 이다 – present
entries.usage: Attach 이다 to a noun to say 'is/am/are' at the right politeness level.
entries.example: 저는 선생님이에요.

entries.point: Past Tense Conjugation of 이다 / 아니다
entries.label: 이다 – past
entries.usage: Attach ~이었/~였 plus a politeness ending to a noun to say 'was/were'.
entries.example: 저는 의사였어요.

entries.label: ~ㄹ/을 것이다 (future)
entries.usage: Add ~ㄹ/을 to the stem, then 것/거 + 이다 to say 'will …'.
entries.example: 저는 밥을 먹을 거예요.

entries.label: Irregulars + ~ㄹ/을
entries.usage: Apply ㅅ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㄹ irregular changes when adding ~ㄹ/을 to a stem.
entries.example: 저는 공원에서 걸을 거예요.

entries.point: Passive verbs with ~아/어 있다 (describing a state)
entries.label: Passive state ~아/어 있다
entries.usage: Turn a passive verb into a 'is currently in this state' form.
entries.example: 문이 잠겨 있어요.

entries.point: Passive/active pairs with 나다 and 내다
entries.label: 나다 / 내다 pairs
entries.usage: Pick the passive (나다) or active (내다) member of the pair.
entries.example: 숙제는 끝났어요.

entries.point: 나다 with nouns (기억이 나다, 화가 나다, 땀이 나다…)
entries.label: Noun + 나다
entries.usage: Say that a feeling, memory or event 'comes up' (subject takes ~이/가).
entries.example: 저는 땀이 나요.

entries.label: Compound verbs (~아/어 + verb)
entries.usage: Join two verbs with ~아/어 to form one compound verb.
entries.example: 남자는 방에 들어왔어요.

entries.label: Sequential ~아/어서
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~아/어서 when the first action leads directly into the second (가다/오다, 앉다/서다/눕다).
entries.example: 우리는 집에 와서 바로 잤어요.

entries.label: Want to (~고 싶다)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~고 싶다, conjugated like an adjective, to say 'want to do'.
entries.example: 저는 내일 쉬고 싶어요.

entries.label: ~고 있다 (progressive)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~고 있다 for an action going on right now
entries.example: 저는 청구서를 지금 확인하고 있어요.

entries.label: ~아/어 있다 (resulting state)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~아/어 있다 for the state left after the action
entries.example: 나는 학교 옆에 서 있어.

entries.label: ~아/어지다 tenses
entries.usage: Conjugate 'become + adjective' like any verb
entries.example: 날씨가 주말에 추워졌어요.

entries.label: ~ㅂ/습니까? (formal question)
entries.usage: Formal high-respect question ending: ~ㅂ니까 after a vowel, ~습니까 after a consonant
entries.example: 매일 아침을 먹습니까?

entries.label: ~니 questions
entries.usage: Informal question ending, usable in all tenses
entries.example: 학교에 가니?

entries.label: ~나(요) soft questions
entries.usage: Softly ask a question with a verb or 있다/없다
entries.example: 지금 밥을 먹고 있나요?

entries.label: ~기 전에
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~기 전에 = 'before doing something'; no tense inside the clause.
entries.example: 저는 자기 전에 이를 닦아요.

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은 후에
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~은 (consonant) / ~ㄴ (vowel) + 후에 = 'after doing'.
entries.example: 저는 숙제를 끝낸 후에 잤어요.

entries.label: 이에요 / 예요
entries.usage: Saying what something is by sticking 이에요 or 예요 straight onto the noun.
entries.example: 이것은 책이에요. — This is a book.

entries.label: Negation 안
entries.usage: The short way to say you don't do something: 안 goes right in front of the verb.
entries.example: 저는 오늘 학교에 안 가요. — I'm not going to school today.

entries.label: 있어요 / 없어요
entries.usage: Saying that something is there or that you have it, and the opposite.
entries.example: 오늘 시간이 있어요? — Do you have time today?

entries.label: 고 싶어요 vs 싶어해요 (I / they)
entries.usage: Saying what you want to do, and what somebody else wants to do.
entries.example: 한국에 가고 싶어요. — I want to go to Korea.

entries.label: (으)세요 requests
entries.usage: Asking someone politely to do something, or talking about someone you look up to.
entries.example: 여기 앉으세요. — Please sit here.

entries.point: Do it for me: 아/어 주세요 (도와주세요)
entries.label: 아/어 주세요
entries.usage: Asking someone to do something for you, as a favour.
entries.example: 문을 열어 주세요. — Please open the door (for me).

entries.point: Can't: 못 vs won't: 안 (못 가요)
entries.label: 못 vs 안
entries.usage: Choosing between not doing it by choice (안) and not being able to (못).
entries.example: 다리를 다쳐서 못 가요. — I hurt my leg, so I can't go.

entries.point: Intention and guessing with 겠 (하겠습니다, 맛있겠다)
entries.label: Intention 겠
entries.usage: Committing to do something yourself, or guessing about something right in front of you.
entries.example: 제가 하겠습니다. — I will do it.

entries.label: Passive & causative 이/히/리/기
entries.usage: Saying something got opened or heard, or that you made someone eat or get dressed.
entries.example: 바람에 문이 열렸어요. — The door was opened by the wind.

entries.label: Plain style 한다
entries.usage: The voice of books, newspapers and diaries, with no politeness ending at all.
entries.example: 한국은 사계절이 있다. — Korea has four seasons. (written style)

entries.point: Future with 되다 (to become) vs 이다
entries.label: 되다 (become)
entries.usage: Saying what someone turns into, and how to say they will be it.
entries.example: 나는 미래에 의사가 될 거야 — I will become a doctor in the future.

entries.label: Guessing 일 거예요
entries.usage: Guessing about somebody else right now: he's probably a doctor.
entries.example: 그 사람이 의사일 거예요 — That person is probably a doctor.

entries.label: Passive ~아/어지다
entries.usage: Saying something got done without naming who did it, when no other passive fits.
entries.example: 좋은 기회가 주어졌어요. — A good chance was given (to me).

entries.label: 들다 (hold / enter)
entries.usage: One verb for carrying something, joining something, falling asleep and liking something.
entries.example: 저는 그 그림이 마음에 들어요. — I like that picture.

entries.label: 가져오다 vs 가져가다
entries.usage: Choosing bring or take by whether you are coming here or going there.
entries.example: 저는 친구 집에 돈을 가져왔어요. — I brought the money to my friend's house (I'm here).

entries.label: 걸리다 (many senses)
entries.usage: One verb for hanging on a wall, getting caught, and taking a length of time.
entries.example: 그림이 벽에 걸려 있어요 — The picture is hanging on the wall.

entries.point: 가지고 있다: to have / to possess
entries.label: 가지고 있다
entries.usage: Saying you have or own something, even though the form looks like 'am having'.
entries.example: 나는 계산기를 가지고 있어. — I have a calculator.

entries.label: 알고 있다 (know)
entries.usage: Saying you know something, and saying 'got it' when you accept what you are told.
entries.example: 나는 그 소문을 알고 있어. — I know that rumor.

entries.label: 잘하다 (good at)
entries.usage: Saying somebody is good at something in general.
entries.example: 제 친구는 노래를 잘해요. — My friend sings well.

entries.label: 못하다 (bad at)
entries.usage: Saying somebody is bad at something in general.
entries.example: 저는 수영을 못해요. — I am bad at swimming.

entries.label: 못 (poorly / couldn't)
entries.usage: Saying you did it badly, or that something stopped you doing it at all.
entries.example: 아니, 못 들었어. — No, I couldn't hear (you).

entries.label: ~지 못하다
entries.usage: The longer way to say couldn't — tacked onto the verb instead of standing in front of it.
entries.example: 저는 어제 자지 못했어요. — I couldn't sleep yesterday.

entries.label: Yes / no questions
entries.usage: Turning a statement into a question with your voice and nothing else.
entries.example: 소식을 들었어? — Did you hear the news?

entries.point: Solid ㄴ additions and the ㄹ irregular
entries.label: ㄹ drop before ㄴ
entries.usage: Dropping the ㄹ off a verb before any ending that starts with ㄴ.
entries.example: 지금 뭘 만드니? — What are you making right now?

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은 다음에 (= 후에)
entries.usage: Saying what you do after finishing something else, with 다음 in place of 후.
entries.example: 숙제가 끝난 다음에 나는 집에 갈 거예요. — After my homework is finished, I will go home.

entries.label: 직전에 / 직후에
entries.usage: Saying it happened right before or right after, not merely before or after.
entries.example: 아들이 저녁 먹기 직전에 과자를 먹었어요. — Right before having dinner, my son ate snacks.

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은 이래로
entries.usage: Saying 'ever since' — correct, though Koreans usually reach for ~ㄴ/은 후에.
entries.example: 한국에 온 이래로 한국어를 배우고 있어요. — Since coming to Korea, I have been learning Korean.

entries.label: Topic 은/는
entries.usage: What the sentence is about: 는 after vowels, 은 after consonants.
entries.example: 저는 학생이에요. — I am a student.

entries.label: Subject 이/가
entries.usage: Who or what does it — new information takes 이/가.
entries.example: 친구가 와요. — A friend is coming.

entries.point: Object particle 을/를 and verb-last order (밥을 먹어요)
entries.label: Object 을/를
entries.usage: The thing acted on: 를 after vowels, 을 after consonants.
entries.example: 밥을 먹어요. — I eat rice.

entries.point: Place and time: 에 vs 에서 (집에, 집에서)
entries.label: 에 vs 에서
entries.usage: Destination/time/being-there = 에; where an action happens = 에서.
entries.example: 도서관에서 공부해요. — I study at the library.

entries.label: 하고 / 도
entries.usage: 하고 joins nouns or means 'with'; 도 replaces the particle to say 'too'.
entries.example: 빵하고 우유를 샀어요. — I bought bread and milk.

entries.label: Comparison 보다
entries.usage: X보다 = more than X; 제일/가장 = the most.
entries.example: 형은 저보다 커요. — My brother is taller than me.

entries.label: ~에 (time or place)
entries.usage: Marking when or where: at three o'clock, to the park, on the sofa.
entries.example: 고양이가 소파 위에 있어요. — The cat is on the sofa.

entries.point: Subject – Object – Adjective form: ~이/가 with adjectives and passive verbs
entries.label: ~이/가 with adjectives
entries.usage: Marking the thing you like, miss or can hear with 이/가 instead of 을/를.
entries.example: 저는 한국 음식이 그리워요. — I miss Korean food.

entries.label: ~보다 + 더
entries.usage: Saying one thing is more than another, and naming what it beats.
entries.example: 형보다 제가 키가 더 커요. — I am taller than my older brother.

entries.label: Destination vs location
entries.usage: Choosing the particle by the verb: 에 for going somewhere, 에서 for doing something there.
entries.example: 저는 공원에 가고 싶어요 — I want to go to the park.

entries.label: Reason 아/어서
entries.usage: Reasons and lead-in sequences; no commands after it.
entries.example: 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요. — I was hungry, so I ate.

entries.label: Reason (으)니까
entries.usage: The reason connector that CAN introduce commands and suggestions.
entries.example: 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요. — There's no time, so go quickly.

entries.label: If (으)면
entries.usage: Conditions and habitual whens.
entries.example: 비가 오면 집에 있을 거예요. — If it rains, I'll stay home.

entries.point: But and and: 지만, 고 (춥지만, 먹고)
entries.label: But / and
entries.usage: 지만 contrasts; 고 lists and sequences.
entries.example: 날씨가 춥지만 갈 거예요. — It's cold, but I'll go.

entries.label: Noun modifiers
entries.usage: Whole clauses describe nouns from the front — Korean's relative clauses.
entries.example: 지금 읽는 책이 재미있어요. — The book I'm reading is interesting.

entries.label: Quotes 다고
entries.usage: Fold what someone said into your sentence.
entries.example: 친구가 내일 온다고 해요. — My friend says he's coming tomorrow.

entries.point: Going somewhere to do: (으)러 가요 (먹으러 가요)
entries.label: Purpose (으)러
entries.usage: Saying where you are going and what you are going there to do.
entries.example: 밥을 먹으러 가요. — I'm going (out) to eat.

entries.label: When (으)ㄹ 때
entries.usage: Saying when something happens — while eating, back when I was young.
entries.example: 밥을 먹을 때 텔레비전을 봐요. — I watch TV when I eat.

entries.label: Background 는데
entries.usage: Setting the scene before a request, or holding two halves of a sentence against each other.
entries.example: 지금 바쁜데 나중에 전화해도 돼요? — I'm busy now — can I call you later?

entries.point: Seems like: 것 같아요 (비가 올 것 같아요)
entries.label: Seems like 것 같아요
entries.usage: Softening what you say to 'it seems' or 'I think' instead of stating it flat.
entries.example: 비가 올 것 같아요. — It looks like it's going to rain.

entries.label: Because 기 때문에
entries.usage: Giving the reason in writing, or in a formal explanation.
entries.example: 일 때문에 못 가요. — I can't go because of work.

entries.point: Quote contractions: 대요, 래요, 냬요, 재요 (온대요)
entries.label: 대요 / 래요 / 재요
entries.usage: Passing on what someone said, asked, told you to do or suggested, the short spoken way.
entries.example: 친구가 내일 온대요. — My friend says he's coming tomorrow.

entries.label: Written connectives
entries.usage: The tighter joining words formal writing uses in place of 고, 지만 and 때문에.
entries.example: 서울은 한국의 수도이며 최대 도시이다. — Seoul is Korea's capital and its largest city.

entries.label: Topic ~는/은
entries.usage: Attach the subject particle, choosing the form by the noun's final sound.
entries.example: 저는 한국 사람이에요.

entries.label: Object ~를/을
entries.usage: Attach the object particle to the noun the verb acts on.
entries.example: 나는 책을 (object) 읽다 – structure practice

entries.label: 이것/그것/저것
entries.usage: Use the demonstrative pronouns as subject or object.
entries.example: 이것은 책이에요.

entries.label: Number + counter
entries.usage: Put a pure Korean number and a counter after the noun being counted.
entries.example: 사람 두 명

entries.point: Counters with numbers (개, 명, 대, 잔)
entries.label: Counters
entries.usage: Number + counter for counting nouns (개, 명, 대, 잔)
entries.example: 저는 펜 네 개를 샀어요.

entries.label: Months of the year
entries.usage: Sino-Korean number + 월 to name a calendar month
entries.example: 제 생일은 3 월 2 일이에요.

entries.label: Topic vs subject particle
entries.usage: ~는/은 for general facts and comparisons; ~이/가 for a specific, just-noticed situation.
entries.example: 산은 높다.

entries.label: 모두 (all / everybody)
entries.usage: Adverbially = 다; as a pronoun it takes particles (모두가, 모두를, 모두에게).
entries.example: 선생님 모두가 회의에 갔어요.

entries.label: 아무나 / 아무도
entries.usage: 아무나 = anybody (positive sentence); 아무도 = nobody (negative predicate required).
entries.example: 집에 아무도 없어요.

entries.label: 아무 + 거/데/때
entries.usage: ~나 for 'anything/anywhere/anytime'; ~도 for 'nothing/nowhere' with a negative verb.
entries.example: 아무 때나 오세요.

entries.label: Noun + ~마다
entries.usage: Attach ~마다 to a noun to mean 'each/every' one of it.
entries.example: 학생마다 달라요

entries.point: Counters: 개, 명, 마리 with native numbers (사과 두 개)
entries.label: 개 / 명 / 마리
entries.usage: Counting objects, people and animals: the thing, then the number, then the counting word.
entries.example: 사과 두 개 주세요. — Two apples, please.

entries.point: 나 vs 저: two words for 'I'
entries.label: 나 vs 저
entries.usage: Choosing the humble 저 or the casual 나 when you say 'I'.
entries.example: 저는 학생이에요. — I am a student. (polite)

entries.point: 번 – counter for times (how many times)
entries.label: 번 (times)
entries.usage: Saying how many times something happened.
entries.example: 저는 어제 학교에 세 번 갔어요. — I went to school three times yesterday.

entries.label: Age 살
entries.usage: Saying how old someone is.
entries.example: 저는 열 살이에요. — I am ten years old.

entries.label: 모든 + noun
entries.usage: Saying every one of something, straight in front of the noun.
entries.example: 모든 아시아 사람들은 젓가락을 잘 써요. — All Asian people use chopsticks well.

entries.point: 있다 with ~이/가: to have, to be at a location
entries.label: 있다 + ~이/가
entries.usage: Mark the possessed thing with ~이/가 before 있다.
entries.example: 저는 커피가 있어요.

entries.point: Turning adjectives into verbs with ~아/어하다 (좋아하다, 싫어하다)
entries.label: ~아/어하다 verbs
entries.usage: Make a feeling-adjective into a verb that can take an object.
entries.example: 저는 맥주를 좋아해요.

entries.point: Comparing with 다르다/비슷하다/같다 and the particle ~와/과/랑/이랑/하고
entries.label: Comparison adjectives (polite)
entries.usage: Say X is different from / similar to / the same as Y using ~와/과
entries.example: 저는 친구와 비슷해요

entries.label: Adjective → noun modifier (~ㄴ/은)
entries.usage: Describe a noun with an adjective or a whole comparison phrase
entries.example: 저는 비슷한 가방을 샀어요

entries.point: Talking about pain and sickness: 아프다 and ~에 걸리다
entries.label: 아프다 (ㅡ irregular)
entries.usage: Say a body part hurts (with 이/가) or that someone was sick
entries.example: 배가 아파요

entries.label: ~적 / ~적으로 / ~적이다
entries.usage: Turn a Chinese-origin noun into a descriptive word, an adverb, or an adjective
entries.example: 그 결정은 경제적이에요

entries.label: ~스럽다 (ㅂ irregular)
entries.usage: Say something has the properties of a noun: lovely, natural, disappointing
entries.example: 그 아기는 사랑스러워요

entries.label: ~스럽다 adjectives
entries.usage: Noun + ~스럽다 makes an adjective; ㅂ-irregular, modifier ~스러운, adverb ~스럽게.
entries.example: 결과는 만족스러웠어요.

entries.label: ~아/어지다 (become + adj)
entries.usage: Adjective stem + ~아/어지다 turns 'be ___' into 'get/become ___'
entries.example: 집 값은 비싸지고 있어요.

entries.label: 낫다 (ㅅ-irregular)
entries.usage: Say 'better' in an explicit comparison; ㅅ drops before vowels
entries.example: 라면보다 밥이 더 나아요.

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은가(요) soft questions
entries.usage: Softly ask about a present state with an adjective or 이다
entries.example: 이 방이 너무 작은가요?

entries.label: 어때 (opinion) forms
entries.usage: Ask someone's evaluation of something, present or past
entries.example: 한국 어때?

entries.label: 또 다른 (another)
entries.usage: Adding one more of something you have already been talking about.
entries.example: 또 다른 문제는 시간이 없어요 — Another problem is that there is no time.

entries.label: 실망하다 vs 실망스럽다
entries.usage: Saying you were disappointed, and naming who or what disappointed you.
entries.example: 저는 친구에게 실망했어요 — I was disappointed in my friend.

entries.label: ~스럽게 adverbs
entries.usage: Describing how something is done: naturally, lovingly, disappointingly.
entries.example: 그는 한국어를 자연스럽게 말해요. — He speaks Korean naturally.

entries.label: 이/그/저
entries.usage: Pick the right 'this/that' word before a noun.
entries.example: 그 사람은 의사예요.

entries.label: Sino-Korean numbers
entries.usage: Combine 일~십, 백, 천, 만 to build numbers for money, time and math.
entries.example: 오천육백

entries.label: Saying zero: 영 vs 공
entries.usage: Pick 영 for math, scores and temperatures; 공 when reciting digits like phone or room numbers.
entries.example: 제 전화번호는 공일공에 일이삼사예요.

entries.label: Clock time (시/분)
entries.usage: Pure Korean number + 시 for the hour, Sino-Korean number + 분 for the minutes
entries.example: 저는 2 시 30 분에 왔어요.

entries.label: Ordinals (번째)
entries.usage: Number + 번째 = first/second/third…, with 첫 for 'first'
entries.example: 저는 세 번째 문을 열었어요.

entries.point: Shortened ordinals: 첫째, 둘째, 셋째, 넷째
entries.label: Short ordinals (첫째)
entries.usage: 첫째/둘째/셋째/넷째 for one's children and for listing points
entries.example: 우리 셋째는 야구를 좋아해요.

entries.label: Months (달/개월)
entries.usage: 두 달 (pure Korean) or 이 개월 (Sino-Korean) for an amount of months
entries.example: 저는 두 달 동안 한국어를 공부했어요.

entries.point: Pure Korean vs Sino-Korean numbers with time counters
entries.label: Number system by counter
entries.usage: Chinese-origin time words take Sino-Korean numbers; native ones take pure Korean numbers
entries.example: 저는 두 달 동안, 즉 이 개월 동안 공부했어요.

entries.point: ~는/은 vs ~이/가: general statements and immediate experience
entries.label: Topic 는/은 vs subject 이/가
entries.usage: Use 는/은 for general or contrastive statements, 이/가 for something specific you are experiencing now
entries.example: 비가 와요.

entries.label: 누구/누가 (who)
entries.usage: Place the 'who' pronoun in the subject, object or pre-이다 slot
entries.example: 누가 그 자리를 차지했어요?

entries.label: 뭐/무엇 (what)
entries.usage: Choose the right 'what' pronoun and decide whether a particle is used
entries.example: 점심이 뭐야?

entries.label: 몇 + counter
entries.usage: Build 'how many ___?' questions with the right counter.
entries.example: 차가 몇 대 있어요?

entries.label: ~는/은 vs ~이/가
entries.usage: Pick the topic or subject particle and the right allomorph.
entries.example: 누가 밥을 먹었어? 내가 밥을 먹었어.

entries.label: 시간 + 후에
entries.usage: Amount of time + 후에 = '___ later / ___ from now'.
entries.example: 저는 세 시간 후에 다시 올게요.

entries.label: 의문사 + ~나 (every-)
entries.usage: 어디나 / 언제나 / 누구나 = everywhere / every time / everyone; no particles.
entries.example: 누구나 실수를 해요.

entries.label: 의문사 + ~ㄴ가 (some-)
entries.usage: 뭔가 / 어딘가 / 언젠가 / 누군가 = something / somewhere / sometime / somebody.
entries.example: 누군가 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.

entries.label: 아무 + 나/도
entries.usage: Build 'any-' words with ~나 and 'no-' words with ~도 plus a negative verb.
entries.example: 아무나 그것을 할 수 있어요

entries.point: Question words: 뭐, 누구, 어디, 언제 (뭐 해요?)
entries.label: 뭐 / 누구 / 어디 / 언제
entries.usage: Asking what, who, where or when — nothing else in the sentence has to move.
entries.example: 지금 뭐 해요? — What are you doing now?

entries.label: 마지막 vs 지난
entries.usage: Choosing the last one at the end of a series, or the one before this one.
entries.example: 이것은 저의 마지막 수업이에요. — This is my last (final) class.

entries.point: 처음 – at first / for the first time
entries.label: 처음 (at first)
entries.usage: Saying 'at first', or that this is the first time something has happened.
entries.example: 저는 처음에 체육 수업을 싫어했어요. — At first I didn't like PE class.

entries.label: 동안 (how long)
entries.usage: Saying how long something went on: for ten minutes, for two days.
entries.example: 저는 10 분 동안 걸었어요. — I walked for 10 minutes.

entries.label: 시간 vs 시
entries.usage: Choosing between the hour on the clock and a number of hours.
entries.example: 저는 세 시간 동안 잤어요. — I slept for three hours.

entries.label: 초 (seconds)
entries.usage: Counting seconds.
entries.example: 저는 2 초 동안 달렸어요. — I ran for 2 seconds.

entries.point: 지난/다음 + time words (last time / next time)
entries.label: 지난 / 다음
entries.usage: Saying last week or next month by putting one word in front of the time word.
entries.example: 저는 지난 주에 영화를 봤어요. — I saw a movie last week.

entries.label: Days 일 / 날 / 하루
entries.usage: Counting days, and the native words for one, two and three of them.
entries.example: 나는 3 일 동안 공부했어. — I studied for 3 days.

entries.label: Weeks 주 / 주일
entries.usage: Counting weeks: 주 or 주일 both work after a number, and 주 is the one you hear more often.
entries.example: 저는 2 주 동안 한식을 안 먹었어요. — I didn't eat Korean food for 2 weeks.

entries.label: 더 (more)
entries.usage: Saying more, without having to name what you are comparing it to.
entries.example: 저는 다음 학기에 더 열심히 공부할 거예요. — Next semester I will study harder.

entries.point: 동안: 'for' a time and 'during' a noun
entries.label: 동안 + noun (during)
entries.usage: Saying 'during' something that is not a length of time: during vacation, during class.
entries.example: 학생들은 수업 시간 동안 조용했어요. — The students were quiet during class.

entries.label: 덜 (less)
entries.usage: Saying something is less than the thing you are comparing it to.
entries.example: 이 영화는 그 영화보다 덜 재미있어요. — This movie is less interesting than that movie.

entries.label: 가장 / 제일
entries.usage: Saying the most, the best, the tallest — one word in front, nothing else changes.
entries.example: 우리 반에서 민수가 가장 키가 커요. — In our class Minsu is the tallest.

entries.label: 잘 (well)
entries.usage: Saying an action was done well this time round.
entries.example: 저는 어젯밤에 잘 잤어요. — I slept well last night.

entries.label: 잘못 vs 잘 못
entries.usage: One space apart: a mistake, or not well.
entries.example: 그것은 제 잘못이었어요. — That was my fault.

entries.label: 왜 (why)
entries.usage: Asking why, by dropping one word into a sentence you already know.
entries.example: 오늘 왜 늦게 왔어요? — Why did you come late today?

entries.label: 언제 (when)
entries.usage: Asking when, and asking since when or until when.
entries.example: 결혼식은 언제야? — When is the wedding?

entries.label: 어디 (where)
entries.usage: Asking where, where to, and how far.
entries.example: 지금 어디 살아요? — Where do you live now?

entries.label: 어떻게 (how)
entries.usage: Asking how something is done.
entries.example: 이 파일을 어떻게 첨부해요? — How do you attach this file?

entries.label: 무슨 + noun
entries.usage: Asking what kind of thing it is when you have no idea at all.
entries.example: 지금 무슨 생각을 해? — What are you thinking about?

entries.label: 어떤 / 어느 (which)
entries.usage: Asking which one, out of a set you can see or already know about.
entries.example: 어떤 로션을 쓰고 싶어요? — Which lotion do you want to use?

entries.point: 무슨, 어떤 and 어느: asking 'what' and 'which' before nouns
entries.label: Choosing 무슨 / 어떤 / 어느
entries.usage: Choosing between the three words that ask 'what' or 'which' in front of a noun.
entries.example: 무슨 소리예요? 밖에서 뭔가 들려요. — What is that sound? I hear something outside.

entries.label: 어떤 (a certain)
entries.usage: Mentioning some person or thing without saying which one it was.
entries.example: 어떤 남자가 어제 우리 집에 왔어요. — Some man came to our house yesterday.

entries.label: 얼마나 (how much)
entries.usage: Asking how much, how often, how quickly, how well.
entries.example: 한국어를 얼마나 자주 공부해요? — How often do you study Korean?

entries.point: 얼마: asking how much something costs
entries.label: 얼마 (price)
entries.usage: Asking what something costs.
entries.example: 이게 얼마예요? — How much is this?

entries.point: Using question words on their own
entries.label: Question words alone
entries.usage: Answering back with just 왜? or 어디? when you need the one detail you missed.
entries.example: 저는 내일 서울에 갈 거예요. – 왜? — I'm going to Seoul tomorrow. – Why?

entries.point: 안 / 이내 (within a period of time)
entries.label: 안 / 이내 (within)
entries.usage: Saying something will happen inside a stretch of time.
entries.example: 나는 5년 안에 외국어 다섯 개를 배우고 싶어. — I want to learn five foreign languages within five years.

entries.label: 다 (completely)
entries.usage: Saying the whole thing got finished, or that everyone in a group did it.
entries.example: 저는 숙제를 다 했어요. — I did all of my homework.

entries.label: 어느 날 (one day)
entries.usage: Naming a vague time or place the way a story does: one winter, some village.
entries.example: 어느 겨울 꽃이 다 사라졌다. — One winter, all the flowers disappeared.

entries.point: 뭐 / 어디 / 누구 as 'something / somewhere / somebody'
entries.label: Bare 뭐 / 어디 / 누구
entries.usage: Using the question words to mean something, somewhere or somebody instead.
entries.example: 아니요. 어디 갔어. — No, she went somewhere.
